text.eyebrow: The cedi and prices · to September 2026
text.lede: When a dollar costs 10% more cedis, imported goods cost about 3% more within three months and about 5% more within a year. Local goods follow almost as much, about 4% within a year, so a weaker cedi raises prices well beyond imports. World fuel and food prices explain only a small part of the 2022 surge. GSS's split between imported and local goods starts in 2021, so this runs from February 2021 to September 2026, and it is recomputed with each release.

text.tile-2-l: for local goods after a year
text.tile-3-l: between the cedi's moves and import inflation, at the closest fit (1–3 months fit almost as well)
text.s1-h2: Import inflation follows the cedi, about two months behind
text.s1-p1: Over a year, import inflation moves most closely with the cedi's change over the year ending two months earlier (a correlation of 0.86; one to three months fit almost as well). Each 10% rise in cedis per dollar goes with about 4.5 more points of import inflation two months later. The cedi's fall peaked in November 2022, when a dollar cost 121% more cedis than a year before. Import inflation peaked two months later, at 62.4% in January 2023. After the cedi's strongest month in the 2025 recovery, June 2025, import inflation kept falling for nine months, to −0.6% in March 2026: the only month in this record when imported goods cost less than a year before.
text.s1-p2: In September 2026 a dollar cost 5.3% fewer cedis than a year earlier. Imported goods cost 2.4% more than a year earlier, and local goods 6.4% more.
text.c1-cap: Change on a year earlier, %, January 2022 to September 2026. Cedis per US dollar: the Bank of Ghana's interbank mid-rate, averaged over each month; a rise means the cedi fell. Imported and local goods: GSS's consumer price index by origin. Hover or tap for any month; Cedi moved two months later slides the cedi's line along to show the lag.
text.c2-cap: Correlation between prices' change over a year and the cedi's change over the year ending 0 to 15 months earlier, January 2022 to September 2026. Highest at two months for imported goods and one month for local goods.
text.s2-h2: About half of a fall reaches import prices within a year
text.s2-p1: Set each month's change in import prices against the cedi's change in that month and in each of the twelve before, and the share passed on builds up like this: 7% in the same month, 20% after one month, 32% after three. Then it slows: 36% after six months and 51% after a year. Local goods follow a similar path, to 44%, and all items to 46%. With five and a half years of data the range is wide: 39–63% after a year for imported goods.
text.c3-cap: Share of a change in cedis per US dollar that has reached prices, by months since the change, %. Shaded: the 90% range for imported goods. Monthly changes, February 2021 to September 2026 (68 months), with each calendar month's usual change taken out.
text.s3-h2: The cedi's three big moves since 2022
text.s3-p1: In the 2022 crash a dollar went from 6.01 to 13.07 cedis, and over the year from January 2022 imported goods rose 62.4%, more than the 40.3% rise the model above predicts. World diesel had risen 66% in the year before, but the section below finds world prices explain only a small part of 2022. In the 2024 slide (11.65 to 15.99 cedis), imported goods rose 18.0%, less than the 27.8% rise the model predicts. In the 2025 recovery (15.53 back down to 10.28 cedis), they fell 0.6%, close to the 2.6% fall the model predicts.

Predicted: what the model behind the chart above gives for imported goods over the same twelve months, from the cedi's moves plus the usual rise in prices that has nothing to do with the cedi.
text.k-cur-sub: euro, yuan and a basket, after a year
text.k-cur: Measured against the euro, 50% of a fall reaches import prices within a year; against the Chinese yuan, 58%; against a basket of the three (half dollar, a quarter each euro and yuan), 54%. The answer barely depends on the currency.
text.k-w22: From March 2023, once the crash had passed through (43 months), the share after a year is 34%, and it builds more slowly: 16% after three months. The 2022 crash pulls the average up.
text.k-asym-sub: of a fall / of a rise, after three months
text.k-asym: After three months, 38% of a fall in the cedi has reached import prices, but only 17% of a rise. After a year the two are close: 46% and 44%. Prices go up faster than they come down. Only 17 of the 68 months saw a stronger cedi, so this is the least certain result here.
text.k-long-sub: all items after a year, 1998 to 2026
text.k-long: All-items prices go back to 1998. Over 1998 to 2026 (329 months), 43% of a fall in the cedi reaches them within a year; over 1998 to 2020, 42%; since 2021, 46%. The recent years aren't unusual.
text.m-data: The cedi. The Bank of Ghana's interbank mid-rate for the US dollar, averaged over each month, in today's cedis. Months with fewer than 10 published rates, and the month in progress, are left out. Prices. GSS's consumer price index for imported goods, local goods and all items: StatsBank before January 2022 for imported and local goods (January 2021 for all items), then the monthly CPI annex, which agrees with StatsBank to its rounding where both exist. Only values that pass TARIN's checks are used. World prices. Diesel: the US Energy Information Administration's daily spot prices at New York Harbor, as FRED (the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) averages them by month, in US dollars a gallon: ultra-low-sulfur diesel since 2006, chained onto No. 2 heating oil before, to September 2026. Food and Brent: the World Bank's Commodity Price Data (the Pink Sheet), monthly, in US dollars: its food price index (2010 = 100) and Brent crude, from the workbook of 2 October 2026, with data to September 2026.
text.m-how: How much, how fast. Each month's change in prices (in logs) is regressed on the change in cedis per dollar in the same month and in each of the twelve before, with a dummy for each calendar month. The running sum of the cedi's coefficients is the share passed on after that many months. Standard errors are Newey–West with four lags; the shaded range is 1.645 of them either side, a 90% range. How many months later. The correlation between prices' change over a year and the cedi's change over the year ending k months earlier, for k from 0 to 15. The cedi or the world. All items, February 1998 to September 2026: the same regression with world diesel and the food index added, each also in the same month and the twelve before. An episode's parts are each one's coefficients applied to its moves, scaled so the parts add up to the change in prices. The range quoted for world prices comes from six other ways of measuring them, Brent instead of diesel among them. What else in 2022. The same regression for each of GSS's 13 groups of the basket (StatsBank, from 1998), each group's parts weighted by its share of the 2021 basket in January 2022.
text.w-h2: World fuel and food prices explain only a small part of the 2022 surge
text.w-p1: GSS's split between imported and local goods starts in 2021: too short to separate the two (see below). Prices as a whole go back to 1998, so the question is asked there. Each month's change in all prices is set against the cedi's change and against world prices of diesel (the US Energy Information Administration's New York Harbor price) and of food (the World Bank's index), in dollars, in the same month and each of the twelve before. Over these 28 years, a 10% rise in world diesel adds about 0.9% to Ghana's prices within a year, and a 10% rise in world food about 0.4%, a figure too uncertain to tell from zero. The cedi's own share hardly moves: 43% within a year, against 43% without world prices. Diesel rather than crude oil, because Ghana imports refined fuel: over the 2022 crash year world diesel rose 25%, while Brent crude fell 3%.
text.w-p2: In the 2022 crash year all prices rose 53.6%. By this measure the cedi accounts for about 21 points of that, and world fuel and food together for about 6 (4 to 8, whichever world prices are used), though world diesel had risen 66% in the year before. About 11 points is the usual rise in prices, in a year when neither moves. That leaves about 15 points that neither the cedi nor world prices explain; the next section looks for them. In the 2024 slide world prices played almost no part (under a point). In the 2025 recovery the cedi's strengthening would have cut prices by about 13 points; they still rose 3.2%, with about 8 points explained by neither.

text.w-cap: All items: the change in prices over the twelve months from each episode's start, split into parts that add up to it, in percentage points (rounding can leave them a tenth apart). Usual rise: what prices do in a year when neither the cedi nor world prices move. The cedi, world fuel, world food: their moves in that year and the twelve months before, at their average effect from 1998 to 2026. Neither: what's left. World prices, in US dollars: diesel at New York Harbor ($ a gallon; ultra-low-sulfur since 2006, No. 2 heating oil before; EIA, via FRED) and the World Bank's food price index.
text.w-p3: For imported goods alone, adding world prices raises the cedi's share to 54–59% within a year, against 51% without them. But five and a half years can't pin down world prices' own effect on them: depending on how they're entered, world diesel's comes out between 6% and 15%, and food's between −11% and 4%, and a negative effect can't be right. So the world is measured on all items only.
text.m-limits: What it leaves out. Freight costs and policy (the Bank of Ghana's rate, fuel taxes and levies, utility tariffs, transport fares) aren't in the model, so part of any episode can be them; for 2022, the section on what else happened lists them without measuring their size. World fuel and food prices are measured for all items only: GSS's import split is too short. GSS's imported goods are a basket of consumer goods priced in shops, not prices at the border. And every share here is an average over the years measured, not a forecast.
text.e-h2: Most of the rest of 2022 is in food, housing and transport
text.e-p1: After the usual rise, the cedi and world prices, about 15 points of 2022's 53.6% rise are left. Fitting the same model to each of GSS's 13 groups of the basket shows where they sit: food and drink about 8 points, housing and utilities about 3 and transport about 3, with the other ten groups adding about 2 between them. 88% of it had built up by July 2022, before the cedi's steepest fall, in October and November 2022.

text.e-cap: The year from January 2022 to January 2023. Weight: the group's share of GSS's 2021 basket. Points added: its rise times its share of the basket at the start, so the groups add up to the rise in all prices: 53.7%, against 53.6% in GSS's all-items index. Not explained: what the group's own fit (the usual rise, the cedi, world diesel and food) leaves over, in the same points. Fitted one group at a time, they add up to 16.6, a little more than the 15.5 of the single all-items fit above.
text.e-p3: One region stands out. Housing and utilities in Greater Accra rose 126% over the year, against 47% in the other regions, which on its own adds about 3 points. And GSS's own housing figures disagree in early 2022: weighted by the basket, its regional indices run up to 20% above the national one (in June 2022), and the two agree again from September 2022, when the national index jumps 17% in a month. Over the whole year they come closer (71% national, 77% from the regions, a difference of 0.6 of a point in 2022's rise), so the year's split holds, but how housing moved month by month in 2022 is uncertain.
text.e-p5: Food rose most in Eastern (80%), Central (73%) and Bono (73%), and least in Volta (36%) and Upper East (38%). On average it rose about 8 points more in the south and middle of the country than in the five northern regions, where much of the grain is grown: what you'd expect if moving food to market got dearer, though TARIN's data can't measure that.
text.e-p4: Two other explanations don't hold up. Big falls of the cedi don't reliably pass through more than usual: in the year from January 2000, when a dollar came to cost 94% more cedis, prices rose about 6 points more than this model gives, but in the year from January 2014 (cedis per dollar up 41%) about 10 points less. And money wasn't racing ahead: broad money grew about 15% a year in early 2022, half its usual pace, and sped up only after prices had (checked in October 2026; StatsBank's money figures stop in mid-2024).
